# An In-Depth Review of *Middlemarch* by George Eliot

## "The History of Man's Condition Has Not Yet Been Written"

---

## Preface: Why *Middlemarch* Demands Our Sustained Attention

There is a particular kind of novel that does not merely tell a story but constructs a world so complete, so morally intricate, and so psychologically penetrating that the reader emerges from it changed — not in the dramatic, sudden way of a revelation, but in the slow, accumulating way of genuine education. George Eliot's *Middlemarch: A Study of Provincial Life*, published in installments between 1871 and 1872, is precisely such a novel. Virginia Woolf called it "one of the few English novels written for grown-up people." Henry James, who was not given to easy praise, described it as "a treasure-house of detail, but... an indifferent whole" — a judgment that, while famously wrong about the whole, at least acknowledged the extraordinary richness of the parts. More than 150 years after its publication, *Middlemarch* remains not only the greatest English novel of the nineteenth century but one of the most searching examinations of human consciousness, social constraint, moral ambition, and the quiet heroism of ordinary life ever committed to prose.

This review will attempt to do justice to the novel's extraordinary scope: its narrative architecture, its thematic preoccupations, its stylistic innovations, its historical and biographical contexts, and its enduring relevance. I will argue that *Middlemarch* is not merely a Victorian artifact but a living document — a text that speaks with uncanny directness to questions we are still asking about gender, vocation, idealism, marriage, community, and the relationship between private conscience and public life.

---

## Part One: The Author and Her World

### George Eliot: The Mind Behind the Novel

To understand *Middlemarch*, one must first understand something of the extraordinary mind that produced it. George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans (1819–1880), and the adoption of that masculine pseudonym was itself a statement about the world she inhabited — a world in which women's intellectual work was systematically devalued, in which a woman who wrote philosophy or fiction under her own name risked being dismissed as a curiosity or a scandal. Evans was, by any measure, one of the most formidably educated people of her era. She had taught herself Latin, Greek, German, Italian, and French. She had translated Strauss's *Das Leben Jesu* and Feuerbach's *Das Wesen des Christenthums* — works of radical biblical criticism that contributed to her loss of Christian faith and her embrace of a secular humanism that would become the philosophical bedrock of her fiction. She had worked as a journalist and editor at the *Westminster Review*, one of the leading intellectual journals of the day, where she engaged with the most advanced scientific, philosophical, and political thought of her time.

She was also, by the standards of Victorian respectability, a social outcast. Her relationship with the philosopher and critic George Henry Lewes — a married man who could not obtain a divorce under English law — meant that she lived in a state of permanent social semi-exile. She and Lewes considered themselves married in every meaningful sense, and their partnership was one of the great intellectual collaborations of the century. But the scandal of their union meant that many respectable women refused to call on her, that she was excluded from certain social circles, and that she lived with a constant awareness of the gap between social convention and genuine moral seriousness. This awareness — of the way society's rules can crush individual aspiration, of the way women in particular are forced to channel their energies into narrow channels — is everywhere in *Middlemarch*.

By the time she began writing *Middlemarch* in 1869, Evans was fifty years old, at the height of her powers, and had already produced *Adam Bede* (1859), *The Mill on the Floss* (1860), *Silas Marner* (1861), and *Middlemarch*'s immediate predecessor, *Romola* (1863). She was, in other words, a mature artist who had spent decades thinking about the relationship between individual consciousness and social structure, between moral aspiration and practical limitation, between the life one imagines and the life one actually lives.

### The Historical Moment

*Middlemarch* is set in the years 1829–1832, a period of intense political and social ferment in England. The Reform Act of 1832, which would extend the franchise and begin the long process of democratizing British political life, was being debated with enormous passion. The railways were beginning to transform the physical and economic landscape. Medical science was undergoing a revolution, with new ideas about contagion, anatomy, and the organization of hospitals challenging entrenched professional interests. The Evangelical movement was reshaping religious life. The question of what England was becoming — what kind of society it would be — was genuinely open.

Eliot chose this moment with great deliberateness. Writing in the early 1870s, looking back forty years, she could see both the promise and the disappointment of that reforming era. The Reform Act had passed, but England remained deeply unequal. Medicine had advanced, but the medical profession remained resistant to innovation. Women's lives had changed very little. The gap between aspiration and achievement — between what the reforming spirit of the 1830s had promised and what it had actually delivered — was a gap that Eliot understood intimately, both historically and personally.

---

## Part Two: The Architecture of the Novel

### Structure and Scope

*Middlemarch* is a novel of extraordinary structural ambition. It began as two separate projects — one centered on Dorothea Brooke, the other on the young doctor Tertius Lydgate — which Eliot eventually recognized as belonging together, as two variations on a single theme. The result is a novel with not one but four major narrative strands, each of which illuminates the others:

1. **Dorothea Brooke's story**: Her disastrous marriage to the elderly scholar Edward Casaubon, her widowhood, and her eventual marriage to Will Ladislaw.

2. **Tertius Lydgate's story**: The idealistic young doctor's arrival in Middlemarch, his medical ambitions, his fatal marriage to Rosamond Vincy, and his gradual defeat.

3. **Fred Vincy and Mary Garth's story**: A more comic, domestic narrative of a young man's moral education and his eventual worthiness of the woman he loves.

4. **Nicholas Bulstrode's story**: The rise and fall of the town's most powerful banker and Evangelical hypocrite, whose hidden past eventually destroys him.

These four strands are woven together with extraordinary skill. Characters from one plot appear in others; events in one narrative have consequences in another; the same social world — the town of Middlemarch and its surrounding countryside — is seen from multiple angles. The effect is of a genuinely social novel, one in which no individual life can be understood in isolation from the web of relationships, obligations, gossip, money, and power that constitutes community life.

The novel is divided into eight "Books," each with a title that signals its thematic concerns: "Miss Brooke," "Old and Young," "Waiting for Death," "Three Love Problems," "The Dead Hand," "The Widow and the Wife," "Two Temptations," "Sunset and Sunrise." These titles are not merely decorative; they organize the reader's attention and signal the novel's preoccupation with time, with the relationship between generations, with the way the past constrains the present.

### The Narrator

One of the most distinctive features of *Middlemarch* is its narrator — a presence so intelligent, so morally serious, and so stylistically distinctive that it constitutes one of the great achievements of English prose. The narrator of *Middlemarch* is not a character in the story; she (and the narrator's voice is unmistakably feminine, though never explicitly gendered) is an observer, a commentator, a philosopher, and occasionally a judge. She moves between the intimate interiority of individual consciousness and the broad perspective of social and historical analysis with extraordinary fluency.

The narrator's relationship to her characters is complex and deeply humane. She is capable of irony — sometimes devastating irony — but she is never merely satirical. She understands her characters from the inside, even when she is most critical of them. Her treatment of Casaubon is perhaps the most remarkable example of this: he is, in many ways, a figure of fun — a dried-up pedant who has wasted his life on a scholarly project that is already obsolete — but the narrator insists that we see him from the inside, that we understand his fear, his wounded pride, his genuine if limited love for Dorothea. The famous passage in which the narrator asks us to imagine "what it would be to have a man's peculiar mixture of egoism and diffidence" — to see the world through Casaubon's eyes — is one of the most morally demanding moments in English fiction. It asks us to extend our sympathy to someone we might otherwise simply dismiss.

This is the narrator's characteristic move: to complicate our judgments, to insist on the full humanity of even the most limited or culpable characters, to remind us that "there is no creature whose inward being is so strong that it is not greatly determined by what lies outside it." The narrator of *Middlemarch* is, in this sense, a practitioner of what we might now call radical empathy — not the sentimental empathy that simply identifies with the sympathetic, but the harder, more demanding empathy that insists on understanding even those we find it difficult to like.

---

## Part Three: The Major Themes

### Theme One: The Problem of Vocation — What Can a Life Become?

The Prelude to *Middlemarch* is one of the most famous passages in English literature, and it is worth quoting at length because it establishes the novel's central preoccupation:

> "Who that cares much to know the history of man, and how the mysterious mixture behaves under the varying experiments of Time, has not dwelt, at least briefly, on the life of Saint Theresa, has not smiled with some gentleness at the thought of the little girl walking forth one morning hand-in-hand with her still smaller brother, to go and seek martyrdom in the country of the Moors? Out they toddled from rugged Avila, wide-eyed and helpless-looking as two fawns, but with human hearts, already beating to a national idea; until domestic reality met them in the shape of uncles, and turned them back from their great resolve. That child-pilgrimage was a fit beginning. Theresa's passionate, ideal nature demanded an epic life: what were many-volumed romances of chivalry and the social conquests of a brilliant girl to her? Her flame quickly burned up that light fuel; and, fed from within, soared after some illimitable satisfaction, some object which would never justify weariness, which would reconcile self-despair with the rapturous consciousness of life beyond self. She found her epos in the reform of a religious order."

> "That Spanish woman who lived three hundred years ago, was certainly not the last of her kind. Many Theresas have been born who found for themselves no epic life wherein there was a constant unfolding of far-resonant action; perhaps only a life of mistakes, the offspring of a certain spiritual grandeur ill-matched with the meanness of opportunity; perhaps a tragic failure which found no sacred poet and sank unwept into oblivion. With dim lights and tangled circumstance they tried to shape their thought and deed in noble agreement; but after all, to common eyes their struggles seemed mere inconsistency and formlessness; for these later-born Theresas were helped by no coherent social faith and order which could perform the function of knowledge for the ardently willing soul. Their ardour alternated between vague ideals and common yearning, between a vague idealism and the common yearning of womanhood; so that the one was disapproved as extravagance, and the other condemned as a lapse."

This passage announces the novel's central subject: the problem of what happens to a great soul — specifically, a great female soul — when the social structures that might channel and sustain that greatness are absent or actively hostile. Dorothea Brooke is Eliot's "later-born Theresa," a woman of passionate idealism and genuine intellectual capacity who finds herself in a world that offers her no adequate outlet for her energies.

The question of vocation — of what a life can become, of how individual aspiration meets social possibility — is not only Dorothea's problem. It is also Lydgate's. The young doctor arrives in Middlemarch with genuine scientific ambitions: he wants to discover the "primitive tissue" that underlies all organic life, to contribute to the great project of medical science. He is, in his way, as idealistic as Dorothea. And he is, in his way, equally defeated — not by the limitations of his sex, but by the limitations of his class assumptions, his vanity, and his catastrophic marriage.

The parallel between Dorothea and Lydgate is one of the novel's great structural achievements. Both are idealists. Both make disastrous marriages. Both are defeated by the gap between their aspirations and the social world they inhabit. But the nature of their defeat is different, and that difference is gendered. Lydgate's defeat is partly his own fault — his condescension toward women, his assumption that Rosamond will be a decorative helpmate rather than a person with her own will, is a form of moral blindness that contributes to his ruin. Dorothea's defeat is more purely social: she is simply not allowed to do what she might have done. The novel's famous Finale makes this explicit:

> "Her finely touched spirit had still its fine issues, though they were not widely visible. Her full nature... spent itself in channels which had no great name on the earth. But the effect of her action on those around her was incalculably diffusive: for the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts; and that things are not so ill with you and me as they might have been, is half owing to the number who lived faithfully a hidden life, and rest in unvisited tombs."

This is one of the most debated passages in the novel. Some readers find it consoling — a recognition that ordinary, unrecorded goodness matters. Others find it deeply melancholy, even tragic — a recognition that the social structures that prevent women from achieving "historic" greatness are a genuine loss, not only for the women themselves but for the world. I think Eliot intends both readings simultaneously. The Finale is not a comfortable resolution; it is a complex, ambivalent acknowledgment of what has been lost and what has been preserved.

### Theme Two: Marriage — The Institution and Its Discontents

*Middlemarch* contains three major marriages (Dorothea and Casaubon, Lydgate and Rosamond, Fred and Mary) and one minor one (Bulstrode and Harriet), and it examines marriage with a thoroughness and psychological acuity that has rarely been matched in fiction. Marriage in *Middlemarch* is not primarily a romantic institution; it is a social, economic, and psychological one. It is the primary mechanism by which women's lives are determined, and it is also the primary arena in which character is tested and revealed.

The Dorothea-Casaubon marriage is the novel's central relationship, and it is one of the most devastating portraits of marital disappointment in literature. Dorothea marries Casaubon because she believes he will be her teacher, her guide to the great world of learning and ideas that she has been denied by her sex and her education. She imagines their marriage as a kind of intellectual partnership, a collaboration in the great work of scholarship. What she gets is something very different: a man who is not only incapable of the intellectual partnership she imagines but who is actively threatened by her intelligence and her energy. Casaubon's jealousy of Dorothea's vitality — his resentment of her capacity for enthusiasm, her ability to find joy in things he cannot — is one of the novel's most psychologically precise observations. He does not want a partner; he wants a worshipper. And when Dorothea proves incapable of the kind of uncritical adoration he requires, he withdraws into a cold, wounded pride that makes their marriage a kind of emotional prison.

What makes Eliot's treatment of this marriage so remarkable is that she refuses to make it simply a story of a villain and a victim. Casaubon is not a villain; he is a limited, frightened, deeply unhappy man who has made the mistake of marrying someone far more alive than he is. And Dorothea is not simply a victim; she has made her own mistake, projecting onto Casaubon a greatness he never possessed, seeing in him what she wanted to see rather than what was there. The novel is merciless about the way idealism can become a form of self-deception, a way of avoiding the actual complexity of other people.

The Lydgate-Rosamond marriage is, in some ways, even more devastating, because it is a marriage between two people who are both, in their different ways, deeply selfish — though neither recognizes this about themselves. Lydgate is attracted to Rosamond because she is beautiful and accomplished and seems to embody a certain ideal of femininity. He does not take her seriously as a person; he assumes she will adapt herself to his needs and his ambitions. Rosamond, for her part, has married Lydgate because she believes he will give her the social position and material comfort she desires. She has no interest in his medical ambitions; she actively undermines them when they conflict with her own desires. The result is a marriage of mutual incomprehension and mutual resentment that destroys Lydgate's career and his spirit.
